text: In a zoneless application (provideZonelessChangeDetection), which of the following schedule a change detection run? (Select all that apply.)
options: An async pipe receiving a new emission
Calling ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()
Setting a signal that is read in a component template
A Promise.then callback that mutates a plain field
Updating a plain class field inside a setTimeout callback
hint: Zoneless relies on explicit notifications, not on patched async APIs.
explanation: Signals read in templates, markForCheck, async pipe emissions and template event listeners notify the scheduler. Plain field mutations in timers or promises produce no notification without Zone.js, so the view stays stale.

text: Which of the following mark an OnPush component view as dirty? (Select all that apply.)
options: A DOM event handler bound in the component's own template runs
An async pipe in its template receives a new value
An @Input receives a new object reference
A property of an input object is mutated in place by the parent
A plain field is changed by a setTimeout callback in the component
hint: OnPush reacts to references and explicit events, not mutation.
explanation: New input references, template-bound events, and async pipe emissions (via markForCheck) dirty the view. In-place mutation keeps the same reference, and a timer changing a field does not mark the view dirty.

text: What happens when signal.set() is called with a value equal (Object.is) to the current value using the default equality?
options: Computed signals recompute but templates are not refreshed
The signal version increments and consumers are marked dirty
Dependents are not notified and no recomputation occurs
Effects re-run once but computed signals are skipped
hint: Default equality short-circuits notifications.
explanation: The signal compares with Object.is and, if equal, does nothing, so no consumers are dirtied. Effects and computeds are consumers and are not notified either.

text: How does a computed() signal behave with respect to evaluation?
options: It recomputes eagerly on every dependency change
It recomputes on every change detection pass
It recomputes on every read regardless of dependency changes
It is lazy and memoized: it recomputes only when read after a dependency changed
hint: Think pull-based, not push-based.
explanation: Computeds are lazily evaluated and cached until a dependency marks them stale. They are not eager, and they do not recompute on each read when dependencies are unchanged.

text: Which statements about effect() in Angular are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Setting a signal always runs dependent effects immediately before set() returns
Effects must always be destroyed manually with destroy() or they leak, even in components
The onCleanup callback runs before the next execution and on destroy
Signals read inside untracked() do not become dependencies of the effect
Effects are scheduled and flushed asynchronously, not synchronously when a signal is set
hint: Effects are reactive side effects with managed lifetimes.
explanation: Effects are batched and run during change detection or the scheduler flush, with cleanups between runs, and untracked reads add no dependency. They do not run synchronously inside set(). Effects created in an injection context are destroyed automatically with their owner, so manual destroy is not required.

text: A component declares a service in viewProviders. Which consumer can NOT inject it?
options: The component itself
A component projected through <ng-content> into this component's template
A directive on an element inside this component's template
A child component declared in this component's template
hint: viewProviders are visible only to the view, not content.
explanation: viewProviders are visible to the component and nodes in its own view but hidden from projected content, which belongs to the parent's declaration. Providers in 'providers' are visible to content children too.

text: A component provides FormStateService in its providers and a child component needs the parent component's instance, while the child itself also provides FormStateService. How does the child obtain the parent's instance?
options: inject(FormStateService, { host: true, self: true })
inject(FormStateService, { optional: true })
inject(FormStateService, { skipSelf: true })
inject(FormStateService, { self: true })
hint: Skip the node's own injector.
explanation: skipSelf starts resolution at the parent element injector. self restricts to the node itself and would return the child's own instance, and optional only changes failure behavior.

text: Which statements about providedIn: 'root' services are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: A lazy-loaded route that injects one gets a new instance per route by default
They are tree-shakable if never injected
They are registered by listing them in AppModule providers
A lazy route's providers array can override them for that subtree
They are singletons in the root environment injector unless overridden
hint: Think about where the root injector sits relative to route injectors.
explanation: providedIn root registers a tree-shakable factory in the root injector, so one instance is shared, including lazy routes, unless a route's providers override it. No per-route instance is created unless the route provides its own.

text: Services listed in a Route's providers array are scoped how?
options: To an environment injector created for that route and its child routes
To the root injector globally
To the component rendered by the route only
To the router-outlet element injector
hint: Routes can create their own environment injectors.
explanation: Route providers create a route-level EnvironmentInjector shared by the route and its children. They are not global, and they are not element-level providers of the component.

text: Which are required or correct when implementing a custom ControlValueAccessor? (Select all that apply.)
options: writeValue is called by the forms API to push model values into the view
registerOnChange stores a function to call when the user changes the value
Provide NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR with useExisting (forwardRef) and multi: true
writeValue should call onChange so the model stays in sync
Call the registered onTouched callback when the control is blurred
hint: Direction of data flow matters for each method.
explanation: The token provider, writeValue (model to view), onTouched, and onChange (view to model) are all part of the contract. Calling onChange inside writeValue would echo the change back and incorrectly mark the control dirty.

text: When is the optional ControlValueAccessor.setDisabledState called?
options: Whenever writeValue is called
When the control becomes invalid
When the bound control's disabled status changes, for example via control.disable()
Only once when the form is first created
hint: It mirrors the control's enabled/disabled state.
explanation: Forms calls setDisabledState to reflect enable/disable calls on the control. It is unrelated to validity or to value writes.

text: After ViewContainerRef.createComponent for an OnPush component, how should a parent supply an input so ngOnChanges and the view update correctly?
options: componentRef.instance.name = value
Object.assign(componentRef.instance, { name: value })
componentRef.changeDetectorRef.detach()
componentRef.setInput('name', value)
hint: There is an API that behaves like a template binding.
explanation: setInput marks the view dirty and triggers input handling like a binding. Assigning to the instance bypasses ngOnChanges and does not mark an OnPush view for check.
code:
const ref = vcr.createComponent(CardComponent);
ref.setInput('name', 'Ada');

text: A component is created with createComponent(Comp, { environmentInjector, hostElement }) outside any view container. What is needed for it to be change-detected?
options: appRef.attachView(ref.hostView), and destroy it when done
Nothing; it is automatically attached to the ApplicationRef
Call NgZone.run once at creation
Add it to the declarations of the root module
hint: Who owns the view's change detection?
explanation: A component created standalone is not part of any tree until its host view is attached to ApplicationRef; it must also be destroyed manually. It is not auto-attached, and zone runs or declarations do not attach it.
code:
const ref = createComponent(Toast, { environmentInjector: this.envInjector, hostElement: el });
this.appRef.attachView(ref.hostView);

text: Which statements about Angular hydration are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: ngSkipHydration opts a component out of hydration
It requires ngSkipHydration on every component
Manual DOM manipulation of Angular-owned nodes can cause hydration mismatches
It reuses server-rendered DOM instead of recreating it
Hydration discards the server HTML and re-renders everything
hint: Hydration relies on server and client DOM matching.
explanation: Hydration reuses existing DOM and requires structure to match, so direct manipulation can break it; ngSkipHydration opts out. It does not discard the server output, and ngSkipHydration is only an opt-out, not a requirement.

text: How does withHttpTransferCache help an SSR app?
options: It disables HTTP requests on the server
It converts HttpClient to the fetch API
Server HttpClient responses are serialized into the page and reused by the client, avoiding duplicate requests
It caches all responses in localStorage permanently
hint: Think about duplicate fetches after hydration.
explanation: Responses made on the server are stored in TransferState and replayed on the client for matching requests. It is not persistent browser storage and does not stop server requests.

text: Which practices keep code safe for server-side rendering? (Select all that apply.)
options: Inject DOCUMENT instead of using the global document
Assume ngOnInit only runs in the browser
Avoid unbounded timers that keep the server render from stabilizing
Guard browser-only APIs with isPlatformBrowser or run them in afterNextRender
Access window or document directly in constructors
hint: The server has no window and waits for stability.
explanation: Platform guards, afterNextRender (browser only), and DOCUMENT injection keep code portable, and pending macrotasks delay stability. Constructors and ngOnInit run on the server too, so global browser access breaks there.

text: How is a custom preloading strategy implemented to preload only routes flagged in data?
options: Implement PreloadingStrategy.preload(route, load) returning load() or of(null) based on route.data
Override Router.navigate to prefetch chunks
Add providedIn: 'root' to the lazy route's component
Use canMatch to return true for flagged routes
hint: The strategy decides whether to call the loader.
explanation: preload receives the route and a loader function; returning load() fetches the chunk and of(null) skips it. canMatch gates matching, not background preloading.

text: Which statements about @defer blocks are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: A standalone component also referenced eagerly elsewhere is still split out into the lazy chunk
on viewport triggers loading when the placeholder enters the viewport
Dependencies used only within the block can be split into a separate lazy chunk
@defer works with NgModule-declared (non-standalone) components in all cases
The @placeholder content is shown before the trigger fires
hint: Deferral depends on how the dependency is referenced.
explanation: Standalone dependencies referenced only inside the block are lazily loaded, but eager use elsewhere keeps them in the main bundle. Placeholders and the viewport trigger work as described. Non-standalone dependencies are not deferrable by default.

text: What does setting "sideEffects": false in a library's package.json allow bundlers to do?
options: Skip type checking during the build
Make the library load lazily at runtime
Drop unused modules/exports during tree shaking
Disable zone patching in the library
hint: It's a promise about import statements having no effects.
explanation: The flag tells the bundler that unused imports can be removed safely, improving tree shaking. It has nothing to do with zones, typing, or runtime lazy loading.

text: What is the difference between shareReplay(1) and shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true })?
options: refCount makes the replayed value expire after one second
Without refCount, values are never replayed
refCount makes the observable hot, otherwise it is cold
Without refCount the source subscription stays open after all subscribers leave; with it the source is unsubscribed at zero subscribers
hint: Think about when the upstream subscription is released.
explanation: Plain shareReplay keeps the upstream subscription alive, which can leak with long-lived sources. With refCount true it unsubscribes at zero subscribers, though replay buffers behave normally in both.

text: Which of these help prevent subscription leaks in components? (Select all that apply.)
options: takeUntilDestroyed() inside an injection context, or with a passed DestroyRef elsewhere
Using the async pipe in the template
Subscribing to HttpClient calls always leaks unless unsubscribed
Calling takeUntilDestroyed() with no argument inside ngOnInit
Storing Subscriptions and unsubscribing in ngOnDestroy
hint: Some operators require an injection context.
explanation: takeUntilDestroyed with DestroyRef, async pipe, and manual unsubscription all release subscriptions. Without an argument outside an injection context it throws, and HttpClient observables complete after the response.

text: By default, what does the share() operator do when the subscriber count falls to zero and a new subscriber arrives later?
options: It keeps the source subscribed forever
It resets and resubscribes to the source, because resetOnRefCountZero is true by default
It replays the last value without resubscribing
It throws an error
hint: share resets by default.
explanation: share() uses a Subject connector and resets on refCount zero, error, and complete, so late subscribers trigger a new source subscription. Replay behavior needs shareReplay or explicit config.
code: const shared$ = source$.pipe(share());

text: Which approaches are appropriate when testing components in a modern Angular app? (Select all that apply.)
options: Use HttpTestingController and call verify() in afterEach
Use component harnesses to decouple tests from DOM structure
Use fixture.componentRef.setInput to set signal inputs
Assign directly to a signal input property on the instance
Use real timers and sleep() to wait for async work
hint: Signal inputs are read-only from the consumer.
explanation: setInput works with signal inputs, HttpTestingController.verify checks outstanding requests, and harnesses abstract DOM. Real sleeps make tests slow and flaky; use fakeAsync or whenStable instead. Signal inputs cannot be assigned directly.

text: Which are sound NgRx-style state design principles? (Select all that apply.)
options: Duplicate derived data in the store for convenience
Mutate state objects in place for performance
Reducers must be pure functions
Normalize entity collections and derive view data through selectors
Keep side effects like HTTP calls in effects, not reducers
hint: Keep state minimal and predictable.
explanation: Pure reducers, normalized state with derived selectors, and side effects in effects keep state predictable. Duplicated derived data goes stale and in-place mutation breaks change detection.

text: When does a memoized createSelector recompute its projector?
options: When any input selector returns a result that is not reference-equal to the previous one
On every store emission
On every change detection cycle
Only when the whole state reference changes
hint: Memoization is by input results.
explanation: A createSelector reruns the projector only if its input selectors' results changed by reference. A new state object alone is not enough if the slices it reads are unchanged.

text: In a Module Federation setup, which configuration choices reduce duplicate Angular runtimes? (Select all that apply.)
options: Declare @angular/core as shared with singleton: true
Give each remote its own bundled copy of Angular
Use strictVersion to fail loudly on incompatible versions
Share the same Router and Injector instance automatically without configuration
Align the Angular versions across host and remotes
hint: One Angular runtime is the goal.
explanation: Singleton sharing, strict versions, and aligned versions avoid duplicate runtimes. Bundling separate copies defeats this, and shared packages do not auto-share injectors.

text: In @for, what does `track item.id` achieve compared with `track $index` when a list is reordered?
options: It sorts the list by id
It makes the iteration lazy
DOM nodes and component instances are moved with their items instead of being rebound to different data
It disables DOM updates entirely
hint: Identity decides what is reused.
explanation: Tracking by a stable id lets the diff move existing views, preserving state. Tracking by index reuses views by position and rebinds them to different items.

text: Which statements about the @for block are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Contextual variables such as $index, $first, $last and $count are available
It only accepts arrays, never other iterables
An @empty block renders when the collection is empty
track is optional and defaults to object identity
The track expression is required
hint: The compiler enforces a track expression.
explanation: track is mandatory, context variables and @empty exist, and it works with any iterable, not only arrays. There is no optional default tracking.

text: A route is lazy-loaded with loadChildren. Which guard prevents the lazy chunk from being downloaded for unauthorized users?
options: canMatch
canActivate
canDeactivate
resolve
hint: Which guard runs while matching, before loading?
explanation: canMatch runs during route matching, so a false result skips the route and its lazy loading. canActivate runs after the route has matched and the chunk loaded; resolve and canDeactivate come later.

text: Which statements about functional route guards are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Returning false cancels navigation without redirecting
They can call inject() to obtain services
Returning a UrlTree redirects navigation
They are skipped for lazy-loaded routes
They must be classes implementing CanActivate
hint: Functions run in an injection context.
explanation: Guard functions run in an injection context, may be async, and results are boolean or UrlTree (sync or async). Class-based guards are not required.

text: When are route resolvers executed relative to guards?
options: After the component is rendered
In parallel with canDeactivate
After guards pass, before the route is activated
Before canMatch
hint: Resolvers need navigation to be allowed first.
explanation: Resolvers run once guards have allowed navigation and complete before activation. They do not run before matching or after rendering.

text: Which are correct when migrating an NgModule app to standalone? (Select all that apply.)
options: All NgModules must be deleted before any component can be standalone
NgModule providers can be brought in with importProvidersFrom
Standalone components cannot import any NgModule
The migration schematic can convert declarations stepwise
Standalone components can import NgModules and other standalone items
hint: Standalone is interoperable with modules.
explanation: Standalone components may import NgModules, importProvidersFrom bridges module providers, and the schematic runs in steps. The cannot-import and must-delete claims are false.

text: The ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError occurs because:
options: In dev mode, a second verification pass finds a binding value that changed during the first pass
Change detection ran twice in production
The component was OnPush
A subscription was left open
hint: It's a dev-mode check.
explanation: Angular re-checks bindings in dev mode and throws if a value changed after being checked, typically due to child-to-parent state changes. It is not produced in production builds.

text: What does ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck() do?
options: Marks only this view and not its ancestors
Marks the view and its ancestors for checking at the next tick without running change detection itself
Runs change detection immediately on this view
Detaches the view from the tree
hint: It schedules, not runs.
explanation: markForCheck marks the path to the root dirty so the next tick checks it. detectChanges is the call that runs it immediately.

text: Which are true of signal-based inputs and model()? (Select all that apply.)
options: Signal inputs can be updated with .set() inside the child
Signal inputs are read-only in the component
input.required() must be provided by the parent or compilation fails
model() enables two-way binding with [(value)]

If the observable errors, reading the signal throws that error
It never unsubscribes automatically

It subscribes immediately and unsubscribes when the owning context is destroyed
hint: It needs an injection context.
explanation: toSignal subscribes eagerly with automatic cleanup, includes undefined without an initial value, and rethrows errors on read. It needs an injection context, not ngOnInit.

text: Which are true about functional HTTP interceptors registered with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...]))? (Select all that apply.)
options: Request handling runs in array order and responses flow back in reverse
They cannot modify the outgoing request
They must return an Observable of HttpEvent
They run in a different order than registered for requests
They can use inject() to access services
hint: Interceptors form a chain.
explanation: Functional interceptors have an injection context, form a chain in order, and return an event stream. Requests are immutable but can be cloned and modified. Claiming that request order differs from registration is false.
